summary:
The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Legislation on equality and public expression is made locally by the Løgting, and the provisions below are Faroese rather than imported.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was set at 18 and stayed there until 1988, when the Løgting adopted a gender-neutral age of 15, eleven years after Denmark made that change.

Since 1 January 2007 a provision has made anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European jurisdiction to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation.

The record documents a gap between that statute and police practice. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented.

A second documented attack dates from 2005, when the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group was not attacked anywhere else on its tour.

Hostility from elected office is documented across a decade. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. The same year av Rana demanded that Pride be banned and repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, documenting organised public pushback alongside the hostility.

Public expression has been contested since the first gay pride march in 2005, which provoked substantial controversy; in 2015 av Rana also suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the city centre.

Partner recognition is unresolved in this record. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at that point the Faroe Islands, with a population of about 47,000, had neither protection nor partnership recognition. No later sourced statement establishes the current status of partnership or marriage registration here.
tangentialFactors:
Petitioning is a recurring feature of Faroese debate and the signature counts are large relative to a population of roughly 47,000. An internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage collected 1,262 signatures.

The Faroese timeline lags Denmark's on age of consent by eleven years (1977 against 1988) and the sourced account places the territory last among Northern European jurisdictions in adopting an anti-discrimination ban, in 2007. These are comparisons of legal milestones, not measures of present-day risk.

The 2006 refusal by police to handle an assault is the clearest documented instance of state machinery failing to act for a LGBT person, and it is tied explicitly to the absence of a statute at that date. Whether the 2007 provision has since been used in prosecution is not documented here.
localsOnly:
The Løgting legislates locally on equality and expression, and the 2007 provision on public threatening, insulting or degrading statements applies to residents as well as visitors, carrying a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

Local party politics carries an explicit institutional position: the Centre Party under Jenis av Rana remains formally opposed to homosexuality, and its leader has sought to have Pride banned and the parade moved out of Tórshavn's centre. The Løgting Speaker used office in June 2015 to attack the national broadcaster's coverage of LGBT Føroyar and a drag show at the Nordic House.

Residents have organised at scale: LGBT Føroyar campaigns locally, and the 2006 petition and street signature drives were run by Faroese residents in Tórshavn shops, tourist centres and petrol stations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current legal status of registered partnership or same-sex marriage in the Faroe Islands is unresolved here: the inventory records the 2006 campaign for a partnership law and a 1,262-signature petition against same-sex marriage, but no sourced statement of the law as it now stands.

No Faroe-specific rules on gender markers in identity documents, passport endorsement, entry screening, facilities access or healthcare provision appear in this inventory; those layers are not sourced and are not asserted.

Enforcement of the 1 January 2007 provision is undocumented: no prosecution, sentence or hate-crime enhancement under it is recorded. The most recent documented episode of official hostility is from 2015 and the most recent documented assault from 2006; no later instances are sourced either way.
